title: Developing an AI Factory Digital Twin with an Agent-Assisted Workflow | NVIDIA Technical Blog
gist: NVIDIA shows an agent-assisted workflow for building an OpenUSD digital twin of an AI factory campus on the Omniverse DSX Blueprint, aimed at the question of how to configure a hall under a fixed power budget. The post is largely an ecosystem showcase (Dassault, PTC, Cadence, Siemens) and its power-efficiency figure is explicitly illustrative, not a modeled result.

themes.theme: Fixed power as the design constraint for AI factories

insights.claim: The framing question for AI factory design is how to configure a hall when available power is fixed, since compute choices change equipment count, placement, electrical distribution and cooling together.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Power, not chip supply, is the binding constraint, so tools that optimize tokens per watt gain strategic value.
insights.quote: How should an AI factory hall be configured when the available power is fixed?
insights.locator: Providing agents with a design foundation

insights.claim: An illustrative Vera Rubin NVL72 comparison normalized to 1 MW at PUE 1.1 shows DSX MaxLPS fitting 400 GPUs and delivering 1.35x the aggregate token throughput of a MaxP baseline (the highest static GPU power setting).
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: If it holds, dynamic power allocation yields about 35% more tokens per megawatt; but NVIDIA says these are reference assumptions, not campus-model results, and Vera Rubin testing is ongoing.
insights.quote: These figures are reference assumptions for the proposed study, not results generated by the campus model.
insights.locator: Extending the campus model to evaluate a fixed power budget

insights.claim: DSX MaxLPS is described as an AI factory design and operating framework coordinating facility design, dynamic power allocation and performance-per-watt optimization.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Positions NVIDIA as defining operating-mode software around its hardware, not just selling racks.
insights.locator: DSX MaxLPS, an AI factory design

insights.claim: Cadence's Reality Digital Twin Platform couples equipment and power models with CFD to simulate MaxP, MaxQ and DSX MaxLPS so stakeholders can see power, cooling and token-throughput effects before a rack is installed.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Pre-build simulation can de-risk capex for multi-hundred-megawatt sites and favors EDA/simulation vendors entering datacenter design.
insights.locator: Cadence Reality Digital Twin Platform answers

insights.claim: Agents given only photos or renderings produce plausible-looking models with possibly wrong dimensions, so useful proposals need grounding in reference assets, site plans, requirements and geographic data, plus dimensional checks and engineering review.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop verification remains the gating step; agents compress iteration but do not replace engineering sign-off.

insights.claim: The workflow runs a frontier model in an agent harness with skills and MCP tool interfaces, uses USD Content Agents to generate geometry such as a solar canopy, and layers changes additively in USD so source assets stay untouched.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Additive layering gives traceable, reversible agent edits, a pattern that would generalize to other regulated design domains.

insights.claim: The team used NVIDIA's Santa Clara headquarters building, Voyager, as architectural inspiration for the example AI factory campus built on the DSX reference design.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Demonstration is a concept model, with the canopy explicitly conceptual, so not evidence of production readiness.

insights.claim: SysML requirement models, if exposed via API or MCP, could let an agent flag dependencies affected by a proposed design change; the post describes this as a proposed workflow, not a delivered one.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Traceability from requirements to geometry is what would make agent-proposed revisions auditable.

insights.claim: SimReady Foundation specifications let teams check whether assets carry the geometry, properties and connection data needed for a given simulation, and agents can surface gaps.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Standardizing asset data readiness is NVIDIA's route to making OpenUSD the exchange layer for datacenter design.

insights.claim: The SimReady Central Library on Hugging Face is a free, ungated library of more than 2,000 simulation-ready OpenUSD assets, including OEM-provided racks, power and cooling equipment.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Free OEM assets lower the barrier for digital twin adoption and tie equipment vendors into the NVIDIA ecosystem.
insights.locator: Developers can also source equipment assets

insights.claim: Dassault Systemes (CATIA Magic, plus A2A support), PTC (Windchill with Omniverse libraries), Cadence and Siemens (Simcenter STAR-CCM+, DSX-aligned reference architectures) are each integrating into the workflow, covering requirements, CAD, CFD and thermal simulation.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Incumbent engineering-software vendors are aligning with NVIDIA's DSX stack, suggesting it is becoming the de facto datacenter-twin platform.

insights.claim: NVIDIA maps hardware to task: DGX Spark for personal agent development, RTX PRO Blackwell workstations for interactive design, DGX Station for larger local models, and RTX PRO Servers (eight RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs per server, four servers per scalable unit) for shared use.
insights.speaker: Ashley Malqui
insights.so_what: Shows NVIDIA pulling simulation and design workloads onto its professional GPU line as a second demand leg beyond training.
